section_summary: This section contains U.S. Embassy Tokyo monthly reports and related State Department memoranda covering January through March 1936. It chronicles the political turmoil surrounding the February 26 military insurrection in Tokyo, including the assassination of key cabinet ministers and elder statesmen, the subsequent court-martial proceedings against Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa, attacks on constitutional theorist Tatsukichi Minobe, and the formation of the Hirota Cabinet. Additionally, it details Japan's withdrawal from the London Naval Conference, ongoing trade and oil disputes with the United States and the Philippines, and escalating border clashes between Japanese-Manchukuo forces and Soviet and Outer Mongolian troops.

subfiles.about: Monthly report on diplomatic, political, and economic developments in Japan during January 1936.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Covers Japanese domestic reaction to President Roosevelt's message to Congress, diplomatic negotiations over Japanese cotton textile shipments to the Philippines, proposed discriminatory automobile manufacturing legislation, foreign oil interests, and the formal withdrawal of the Japanese delegation from the London Naval Conference. In international affairs, it highlights Foreign Minister Hirota's three-point China policy address to the Diet, armed clashes along the Manchukuo-Outer Mongolia frontier, and the establishment of Japanese legations in Addis Ababa and Cairo. Internally, the report reviews the court-martial of Lt. Col. Saburo Aizawa for the murder of Maj. Gen. Tetsuzan Nagata, the dissolution of the Imperial Diet by Premier Okada ahead of general elections, the controversy surrounding Dr. Minobe's institutional theory of the Emperor, and national finance and trade statistics.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of January, 1936 (Report No. 112)

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 113 on conditions in Japan during February 1936, dominated by the February 26 military uprising.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Transmits Embassy Report No. 113 detailing the February 26 military insurrection in Tokyo by young Army officers who assassinated Finance Minister Takahashi, Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal Saito, and General Watanabe, while Premier Okada escaped and Admiral Suzuki was critically wounded. Documents the imposition of martial law, the surrender of the insurgent troops on February 29, the interim appointment of Home Minister Fumio Goto as Acting Premier, and the remarkable stability of financial markets under emergency controls. Also details the February 20 Diet election results favoring the Minseito, the assassination attempt on Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe by a rightist, a severe clash involving tanks and planes near Lake Buir, and ongoing negotiations over textile exports to the Philippines and petroleum storage mandates.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1737, Enclosing Report No. 113 on Conditions in Japan during the Month of February, 1936

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing significant items from the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report for March 1936.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (initialed WHT / WTT)
subfiles.summary: Summarizes selected highlights from the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report for March 1936 for the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. Notes Kensuke Horinouchi's denial that Japan planned an official goodwill mission to the Institute of Pacific Relations conference in Yosemite, California. Details the dispatch of a Japanese economic mission to Siam to answer popular demand for economic expansion southward, and notes the formation of the chauvinistic Kenmu Society by figures including Generals Araki, Masaki, and Hayashi, Mitsuru Toyama, and Prince Konoe.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Embassy's Monthly Report for March 1936
subfiles.to: Secretary of State / Far Eastern Affairs Division

subfiles.about: Embassy despatch transmitting Report No. 114 on conditions in Japan during March 1936, including the formation of the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Transmits Embassy Report No. 114 detailing the aftermath of the February 26 Incident, security measures for foreign embassies in Tokyo, and the formation and policy declaration of the new Cabinet under Prime Minister Koki Hirota. Covers informal representations by Ambassador Grew to Premier Hirota on mounting trade friction over cheap Japanese exports, as well as ongoing discussions between foreign oil companies and Japanese officials regarding the Petroleum Industry Law storage requirements. Chronicles sharp border clashes between Soviet-Manchukuo forces near Changlingtsu and along the Outer Mongolian frontier near Lake Buir, alongside the arrest of Japanese employees of the Soviet Embassy in Tokyo and the seizure of two Soviet ships at Aomori for alleged espionage.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1781, Enclosing Report No. 114 on Conditions in Japan during the Month of March, 1936
